claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in HEA multilayers is primarily governed by the evolution of strain-induced short-range order.
Strain-induced short-range order arises from severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity.
Evolving short-range order modulates local dislocation nucleation and glide and thereby regulates creep.
The proposed starting material is a nanoscale coating with alternating FCC and BCC HEA layers.
The starting FCC/BCC HEA multilayer inherently has significant lattice distortion and pre-existing short-range order.
Post-deposition annealing can reduce or randomize local chemical short-range order relative to the as-deposited coating.
The relevant structural mediator is the formation and evolution of strain-induced short-range order at HEA multilayer interfaces.
Interfacial short-range order locally alters lattice resistance and dislocation mobility.
Sustained applied stress promotes further evolution of short-range order within the HEA layers.
Ordered regions in samples with intact short-range order act as transient barriers to dislocation motion.
Transient dislocation barriers produce more homogeneous and gradual plastic deformation with enhanced strain hardening.
Randomizing short-range order increases dislocation mobility.
Increased dislocation mobility after randomization of short-range order causes more localized plasticity and a higher creep rate.
As-deposited multilayers with preserved short-range order will creep more slowly than annealed, randomized specimens.
As-deposited multilayers will show continuous gradual strain hardening, whereas annealed specimens will show earlier localized deformation.
Creep in conventional metallic multilayers is primarily controlled by ordinary dislocation glide across interfaces without significant modulation by evolving short-range order.
Compositional variation can change the creep or mechanical response of high-entropy alloys.
Loading rate can change the operative creep mechanism in a high-entropy alloy.
Individual layer thickness and testing temperature may alter the proposed response.
No statistically significant creep-rate or strain-hardening difference, or failure of the as-deposited samples to creep more slowly, would falsify the hypothesis.
